extracted.intended_audience: advanced students and researchers in mechanics, history and philosophy of physics
extracted.subtask_description: Critical exposition of the conceptual foundations and methodological criteria for formulating and applying the principles of mechanics (Newtonian and Huygenian), with historical commentary and proposed alternative formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton's Three Laws (I–III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law I. Every body perseveres in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line, except in so far as it is compelled to change that state by impressed forces. Law II. Change of motion [i.e. of momentum] is proportional to the moving force impressed, and takes place in the direction of the straight line in which such force is impressed. Law III. Reaction is always equal and opposite to action; that is to say, the actions of two bodies upon each other are always equal and directly opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as the fundamental dynamical principles from which corollaries (parallelogram of forces, conservation-type statements, centre of gravity motion invariance, relative motion rules) follow. They are to be read together with ensuing corollaries and definitions to apply to mechanical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions from laws; avoid tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws I and II are largely contained in the definitions of force that precede; once acceleration is established as the measure of force it is tautological to restate proportionality of change of motion to force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formulating foundational propositions, be careful not to restate definitional content as empirical laws. Explicitly separate what is a definition (convention/measure) from what is an experimental proposition; otherwise one risks circularity or tautology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third law requires correct concept of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: The third law is unintelligible without the correct idea of mass, and since the idea of mass itself is obtained from dynamical experience, that renders a strictly independent statement of the third law unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the concept of mass is properly defined/established (empirically grounded) before applying or interpreting action–reaction statements; otherwise the third law's content may be vacuous or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental proposition: mutual contrary accelerations along line of junction (proposed a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies set opposite each other induce in each other, under certain circumstances to be specified by experimental physics, contrary accelerations in the direction of their line of junction. (The principle of inertia is included in this.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate as an empirical statement about what bodies do to one another; list the experimental conditions under which the statement holds rather than embedding hidden assumptions about causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: mass-ratio via induced accelerations (proposed b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass-ratio of any two bodies is the negative inverse ratio of the mutually induced accelerations of those bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an operational definition: determine masses by measuring accelerations bodies impart to each other under controlled interaction, rather than assuming an a priori metaphysical property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental proposition: mass-ratios independent of physical states (proposed c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass-ratios of bodies are independent of the character of the physical states (of the bodies) that condition the mutual accelerations produced, be those states electrical, magnetic, or what not; and they remain, moreover, the same, whether they are mediately or immediately arrived at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass should be empirically invariant across different interaction mechanisms and ways of achieving the interaction; tests should check independence from the bodies' physical states and from mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental proposition: accelerations induced by several bodies are independent (proposed d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The accelerations which any number of bodies A, B, C... induce in a body K, are independent of each other. (The principle of the parallelogram of forces follows immediately from this.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multi-body interactions, treat induced accelerations as superposable (vector addition) unless experimental evidence indicates dependence; this justifies the parallelogram composition of forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: moving force as mass times acceleration (proposed e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving force is the product of the mass-value of a body into the acceleration induced in that body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an operational quantitative definition of force (F = m a) that ties the term to measurable quantities (mass, acceleration) rather than to hidden causal entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, parsimony, and clarity as criteria for foundational propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed substitutions satisfy the requirements of simplicity and parsimony which, on economico-scientific grounds, must be exacted of them. They are obvious and clear; no doubt can exist with respect to any one of them either concerning its meaning or its source; and we always know whether it asserts an experience or an arbitrary convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing foundational axioms/propositions prefer formulations that are simple, economical, clearly interpretable, and that transparently indicate whether they are empirical claims or conventions. This aids communication and further development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational/empirical conception of force; avoid hidden causes
rubrics_metrics.description: What is called force in modern mechanics is not a something lying latent in natural processes, but a measurable, actual circumstance of motion, the product of the mass into the acceleration. When speaking of attractions or repulsions we need not think of hidden causes; the term merely signals resemblance between events determined by motion conditions and results of volitional impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret theoretical terms (like 'force' or 'attraction') in operational, empirical terms tied to observable motion. Refrain from positing occult causes when measurable relations suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple equivalent methodological frameworks (force vs work/vis viva)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton operates with the notions of force, mass, and momentum; Huygens pursued work, mass, and vis viva. Both starting points (ft = mv and f·s = mv^2/2) are equally simple and, as starting assumptions, equally admissible; choice depends on problem convenience and investigational preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that different formal frameworks can be equivalent or complementary. Choose the Newtonian (force/momentum) or Huygenian (work/vis viva) approach depending on which yields simpler/clearer treatment for the problem at hand; neither is universally superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mass and weight; empirically motivate mass concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicists were not led to form the concept of mass until they discovered that the same body can by the action of gravity receive different accelerations (e.g., pendulum observations). Newton personally made observations to prove proportionality of mass and weight on the same spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mass as an empirically grounded quantity distinct from weight; validate mass-concepts through experiments (pendulums, comparative accelerations) rather than linguistic habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling extended bodies by aggregates of small portions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several masses have considerable extension so that a single line joining every two masses is impossible, divide masses into portions sufficiently small for the purpose, draw lines of junction between every two such portions, and account for reciprocal relations of parts (elastic forces, resistance to change of internal distances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In continuum or extended-body problems, represent bodies as assemblies of infinitesimal elements and include internal elastic interactions; treat contacts/impacts by considering contact-induced deformation and elastic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and heuristic value: study rejected and transient ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical investigation of the development of a science is most needful, lest the principles treasured up in it become a system of half-understood prescripts, or worse, a system of prejudices. Rejected and transient thoughts may be very important and instructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the history of ideas as a methodological tool to reveal conventional or accidental aspects of current formulations and to suggest alternative routes; do not treat accepted principles as unquestionable dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope criterion: Newtonian principles suffice in principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of Newton suffice by themselves, without the introduction of any new laws, to explore and thoroughly every mechanical phenomenon practically occurring, whether it belongs to statics or to dynamics. If difficulties arise they are mathematical or formal, not of principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When solving mechanical problems, assume Newtonian principles are adequate unless there is experimental evidence to the contrary; focus effort on mathematical/formal techniques to handle complexity rather than inventing new fundamental laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to reformulation (integral vs differential laws; possible superfluity of force)
rubrics_metrics.description: It cannot be regarded as impossible that integral laws may some day take the place of the differential laws that now make up the science of mechanics, and that we shall have direct knowledge of the dependence on one another of the positions of bodies. In such an event, the concept of force will have become superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain openness to alternative mathematical formulations of mechanics; foundational concepts (like force) may be reformulated or become unnecessary in superior frameworks. Evaluate concepts by their explanatory and predictive utility, not by historical inertia.
